This tutorial is intended to assist the user in getting started with calculating centroids of discrete (probability) distributions relative to the Jeffreys and Jensen-Shannon divergences with the package `{igcentroids}` and integrating these computation in a clustering-task workflow. 
It starts with a short, technical presentation of the underlying S3 classes of R objects the package is built upon, in @sec-vig_catdist_presclasses. 
The information-geometric theoretical foundation of the ensueing procedures is outlined in Setions [-@sec-vig_catdist_presdivergences] and [-@sec-vig_catdist_prescentroids]. More precisely, the definitions and properties of Kullback-Leibler (KL), Jeffreys (J) and Jensen-Shannon (JS) divergences (div) and related centroids are reviewed; the usage of methods for computing them is also illustrated. 
These procedures fully integrate into a clustering-task workflow performed with the package `{flexclust}`, as illustrated in @sec-vig_catdist_clustering. 
<!-- Finally, full examples of such clustering tasks are presented in @sec-vig_catdist_fullexamples. -->

As a preliminary step, load the package `{igcentroids}`, as follows.

```{r}
#| label: setup
library(igcentroids)
```

It is implicitly assumed that the package `{igcentroids}` has been previously installed; if not, please, refer to the [README](https://github.com/pregnault/igcentroids) file on top of the repository of the package.


## S3 classes `igccatdist`, `igccatdistn`, `igcmatcatdist` and `igcmatcatdistn` {#sec-vig_catdist_presclasses}

`{igcentroids}` provides several procedures for clustering categorical -- or finite-state space -- (probability) distributions with same support. 

We formally denote $\mathcal{P}(\mathcal{X})$ the set of positive measures -- or categorical distributions -- on the finite set $\mathcal{X} = \{x_1, \cdots, x_d\}$. Such a measure $\mu$ is mathematically identifiable to the vector $(\mu(x_1), \cdots, \mu(x_d)) \in \mathbb{R}^d$ with  $\mu(x_j) >0$  for all $j \in \{1, \cdots, d\}$; it is represented in `{igcentroids}` as an object of S3 class `igccatdist` built upon classical numeric vectors. Such an object is obtained as the output of the eponyme constructor function `igccatdist()`, taking a positive numeric vector as input.

```{r}
#| label: creating_igccatdist_object
set.seed(679)
# A positive measure on a 5-state space
p <- igccatdist(sample(1:10, size = 5L, replace = TRUE))
```

`igccatdist` objects are positive numeric vectors with two attributes `class` and `mass`. The first one is obviously `"igccatdist"` while the second is the mass of the whole set of states i.e., the sum of the components of the vector. Both attributes are displayed when the object is printed.

```{r}
#| label: printing_igccatdist_object
print(p)
```

Note that a validation function prevents the user to convert into `igccatdist` non-positive vectors.

```{r}
#| label: error_non-positive_entries_igccatdist
#| error: true 
igccatdist(c(1, 0))
igccatdist(-(1:3))
```

The subset $\mathcal{P}_1(\mathcal{X}) \subset \mathcal{P}(\mathcal{X})$ of positive measures with mass equal to one is of foundamental interest in any field related to probability theory. Its elements are probability measures, called here normalized categorical distributions; they are represented in `{igcentroids}` as objects of class `igccatdistn`, unformally inheriting from `igccatdist`. 

```{r}
#| label: creating_igccatdistn_object
# The binomial distribution of parameters 
# n = 4 and p = 0.5 as an igccatdist object
q <- igccatdistn(dbinom(x = 0:4, size = 4L, prob = 0.5))
print(q)
# Normalize a positive vector prior to convert it to igccatdistn
p <- undo_igc(p) # Remove class igccatdist to retrieve a numeric vector
igccatdistn(p/sum(p))
```

Sets of (normalized) categorical distributions on the same support are represented as positive matrices -- stochastic matrices for normalized categorical distributions; dedicated classes are introduced in `{igcentroids}` : `igcmatcatdist` and `igcmatcatdistn`.

```{r}
#| label: creating_igcmatcatdist
matcd <- matrix(c(p, q), nrow = 2, byrow = TRUE)
igcmatcatdist(matcd)
matncd <- matrix(c(p/sum(p), q), nrow = 2, byrow = TRUE)
igcmatcatdistn(matncd)
```

The function `bind_igc()` eases the creation of `igcmatcatdist` or `igcmatcatdistn` objects by binding together objects of classes `igc...`. Here are some examples, the class of output depending on whether all inputs are normalized or not.

```{r}
#| label: binding-igc-objs
# binding objects of classes igcmatcatdist and igcmatcatdistn
# results in an igcmatcatdist object.
matcd <- igcmatcatdist(matcd)
matncd <- igcmatcatdistn(matncd)
bind_igc(matcd, matncd)
# Add a row to an igcmatcatdist object
r <- igccatdist(sample(1:10, size = 5L, replace = TRUE))
bind_igc(matcd, r)
# Add a row to an igcmatcatdistn object
s <- igccatdistn(dbinom(0:4, size = 4L, prob = 0.3))
bind_igc(matncd, s)

```


Methods for generics `plot()` and `points()` associated to `igccatdistn` and `igcmatcatdistn` are available. Their behaviour depends on the size $|\mathcal{X}|$ of the support $\mathcal{X}$. More precisely, Two-state and three-state supports benefit of particular representations, for mere of pedagogical purpose, as illustrated by Figures [-@fig-23statencdplot-1] and [-@fig-23statencdplot-2].

```{r}
#| layout-ncol: 2
#| label: fig-23statencdplot
#| fig-cap: Examples of representations of categorical probability distributions obtained with the methods `plot()` and `points()` for `igcmatcatdistn` objects.
#| fig-subcap:
#|   - Two-state probability distributions are represented as points on a unite segment.
#|   - Three-state probability distributions are represented as points in the 2D simplex identified to the equilateral triangle.
# Two-state  categorical distributions plot
u <- c(0.5, 0.5)
p1 <- c(0.3, 0.7)
p2 <- c(0.4, 0.6)
x <- igcmatcatdistn(matrix(c(u, p1, p2),
                     nrow = 3, ncol = 2, byrow = TRUE))
plot(x)
# Three-state categorical distributions plot
runifsimplex <- function(n = 1L) {
  x <- runif(n)
  y <- runif(n, min = 0, max = 1-x)
  res <- igcmatcatdistn(matrix(c(x,y, 1-x-y), ncol = 3, byrow = FALSE))
  return(res)
}
set.seed(527)
sampsimp <- runifsimplex(n = 32L)
plot(sampsimp)
```

Categorical probability distributions with bigger state spaces are represented as polylines i.e., continuous piecewise linear functions linking the top of bars in a classical barplot; see @fig-plotbigstatespacencd.

```{r}
#| label: fig-plotbigstatespacencd
#| fig-cap: The barplot of a 10-state space probability distribution presented as a polyline.
p <- sample(1:10, size = 10L, replace = TRUE)
p <- igccatdistn(p/sum(p))
plot(p)
```



## Computing divergences of a couple of categorical distributions {#sec-vig_catdist_presdivergences}

Divergence functionals constitute a primal notion of information theory and related fields. 
Among them, the Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence of two positive measures is of special theoretical and practical importance due to its axiomatic, structural and geometric properties ; see, e.g [@amari2016]. 
<!-- DEVELOPPER QUELQUES PROPRIETES ? -->
The KL divergence $\mathbb{K}(p|q)$ of a couple $(p, q) \in \mathcal{P}(\mathcal{X})^2$ of positive measures with same support is given by
$$
\mathbb{K}(p|q) := \sum_{x \in \mathcal{X}} p(x) \log \frac{p(x)}{q(x)} - \sum_{x \in \mathcal{X}} p(x) + \sum_{x \in \mathcal{X}} q(x).
$$ {#eq-defkldivposvec}
Altought it is not a proper mathematical distance due to lack of symmetry and triangular inequality, its numerous properties make it a relevant measure of discrepancy between positive measures. First of all, $\mathbb{K}(p | q) \geq 0$ for any couple $(p, q)$ and $\mathbb{K}(p | q)  = 0$ if and only if $p = q$.

Restricted to the set of couples of probability distributions, the two former sums in @eq-defkldivposvec cancel and the KL divergence simplifies to
$$
\mathbb{K}(p|q) = \sum_{x \in \mathcal{X}} p(x) \log \frac{p(x)}{q(x)}, \quad p, q \in \mathcal{P}_1(\mathcal{X}).
$$
The KL divergence of two positive measures can be computed thanks to the function `kldiv()` of `{igcentroids}`:
```{r}
#| label: cpt-kldiv-posvec
set.seed(987)
# KL div for positive vectors
p <- igccatdist(sample(1:10, size = 5L, replace = TRUE))
q <- igccatdist(sample(1:10, size = 5L, replace = TRUE))
kldiv(p, q)
kldiv(q, p) # KL is not symmetric
# KL div for prob. dist.
p <- igccatdistn(dbinom(0:4, size = 4L, prob = 0.3))
q <- igccatdistn(dbinom(0:4, size = 4L, prob = 0.5))
kldiv(p, q)
```

To overcome the lack of symmetry -- that appears to be a serious disagreement for the use of KL divergence for clustering purpose -- several symmetrizations have been proposed in the litterature [@nielsen2019entropy]. The Jeffreys and Jensen-Shannon divergences are the two most notable such symmetrizations. 
Jeffreys divergence of a couple of positive vectors, introduced in [@jeffreys1946] is the sum of KL divergences of the couple $(p,q)$ and its chiral version $(q,p)$:
$$
\mathbb{J}(p, q) := \mathbb{K}(p | q) + \mathbb{K}(q | p) = \sum_{x \in \mathcal{X}} (p(x) -q(x)) \log \frac{p(x)}{q(x)}.
$$
It is extensively used in machine and deep learning as a loss function [@bousquetrouvier2023], [@nguyenetal2017], [@nielsen2013] and in signal processing [@griveletal2018].
<!-- DEVELOPPER. -->

Jensen-Shannon (JS) divergence [@lin1991], whose first appearance dates back to [@wong1985], is the average of KL-divergences from each vector $p$ and $q$ with respect to their arithmetic mean; more precisely,
$$
\mathbb{JS}(p, q) := \frac{1}{2} \left( \mathbb{K}\left((p \Big| \frac{p+q}{2} \right) +  \mathbb{K}\left( q \Big| \frac{p+q}{2} \right) \right).
$$
Besides its symmetry, JS divergence satisfies additionnal properties that make it relevant in numerous applications: it can be defined for categorical distributions with distinct supports, it always lies between $0$ and $\frac{1}{2}(p(\mathcal{X}) + q(\mathcal{X}))\log(2)$ where $p(\mathcal{X})$ and $q(\mathcal{X})$ denote the total weight of the state space $\mathcal{X}$ ($p(\mathcal{X}) = \sum_{x} p(x)$) -- this upper bound being achieved when the supports $p$ and $q$ are disjoint, and it can be expressed as the diferrence between the Shannon entropy of the arithmetic mean of $p$ and $q$ and the arithmetic mean of their Shannon entropies. Finally, the square root of $\mathbb{JS}$ define a proper euclidean metric on $\mathcal{P}(\mathcal{X})$; see [@endresandschindelin2003].

Jeffreys and JS divergences of two positive vectors or categorical distributions can be computed thanks to the functions `jdiv()` and `jsdiv()` in `{igcentroids}`. 

```{r}
#| label: cpt-jjsdivposvects
#| echo: true
#| eval: true
set.seed(587)
# Jeffreys and JS divs for positive vectors
p <- igccatdist(sample(1:10, size = 5L, replace = TRUE))
q <- igccatdist(sample(1:10, size = 5L, replace = TRUE))
jdiv(p, q)
jsdiv(p, q)
# Jeffreys and JS divs for prob. dist.
p <- igccatdistn(dbinom(0:4, size = 4L, prob = 0.3))
q <- igccatdistn(dbinom(0:4, size = 4L, prob = 0.5))
jdiv(p, q)
jsdiv(p,q)
# Both are symmetric
all.equal(jdiv(q,p), jdiv(p,q))
all.equal(jsdiv(q,p), jsdiv(p,q))
```

Methods of `jdiv()` and `jsdiv()` for positive matrices and stochastic matrices are also provided, applying the above functions to all combinations of the rows of the two input matrices and formatting the output as a numeric matrix.

```{r}
#| label: cpt-jjsdivposmat
#| echo: true
#| eval: true
mat1 <- bind_igc(p, q)
r <- igccatdistn(dbinom(0:4, size = 4L, prob = 0.4))
s <- igccatdistn(dbinom(0:4, size = 4L, prob = 0.2))
t <- igccatdistn(dbinom(0:4, size = 4L, prob = 0.1))
mat2 <- bind_igc(r, s, t)
jdiv(mat1, mat2)
jsdiv(mat1, mat2)
```
The second matrix input of `jdiv()` and `jsdiv()` is optional; if not provided, it is implictly assumed to be equal to the first one, making obvious the computation of the "distance" matrix of a set of positive vectors or categorical distributions -- which can further be used as input of classical R functions for clustering; see @sec-vig_catdist_clustering.

```{r}
#| label: cpt-jjsdivsetcd
#| echo: true
#| eval: true
jdiv(mat2)
jsdiv(mat2)
```



## Computing centroids of a set of categorical distributions {#sec-vig_catdist_prescentroids}

Given a set $\{p^{(1)}, \cdots, p^{(n)}\} \subseteq \mathcal{P}(\mathcal{X})$ of $n$ positive vectors of size $d$ assorted with weights 
$\omega_1, \cdots, \omega_n$, the Jeffreys and Jensen-Shannon centroids $c_{\mathbb{J}} = c_{\mathbb{J}}(p^{(1)}, \cdots, p^{(n)})$ and $c_{\mathbb{JS}} = c_{\mathbb{JS}}(p^{(1)}, \cdots, p^{(n)})$ are defined by
$$
c_{\mathbb{J}}  :=  \textrm{Argmin}_{p \in \mathcal{P}(\mathcal{X})} \sum_{i=1}^n \omega_i \mathbb{J}(p, p^{(i)}),
$${#eq-defcentroids1}
and 
$$
c_{\mathbb{JS}}  :=  \textrm{Argmin}_{p \in \mathcal{P}(\mathcal{X})} \sum_{i=1}^n \omega_i \mathbb{JS}(p, p^{(i)}).
$$ {#eq-defcentroids2}
The opmitization set in the definitions (-@eq-defcentroids1) and (-@eq-defcentroids2) is restricted to the set of probability distributions $\mathcal{P}_1(\mathcal{X})$ when  $p^{(1)}, \cdots, p^{(n)}$ are probability distributions; we denote $c_{\mathbb{J}}^{(1)}$ and $c_{\mathbb{JS}}^{(1)}$ such centroids of probability distributions so as to avoid confusion on the optimization set under study.

@nielsen2013 establishes an explicit analytic formula for Jeffreys centroid of positive vectors; precisely, it is given by
$$c_{\mathbb{J}}(x) = \frac{a(x)}{\mathrm{W}\left( \frac{a(x)}{g(x)} e \right) }, \quad x \in \mathcal{X},$$
where $a$ and $g$ denote respectively the arithmetic and geometric centroids given by
$$
a(x) = \sum_{i=1}^n \omega_i p^{(i)}(x), \quad g(x) = \prod_{i=1}^n p^{(i)}(x)^{\omega_i}, \quad x \in \mathcal{X},
$$
and $\mathrm{W}$ is the branch $\mathrm{W_0}$ of the Lambert function, implicitly defined by $\mathrm{W}(x)\exp(\mathrm{W}(x)) = x$ for $x \geq 0$; see [@nielsen2013] for details.
This closed form of Jeffreys centroid of positive vectors is returned by the method `jcent()` associated with the class `igcmatcatdist`. It returns an object of class `igccatdist`, as illustrated in the following chunk.

```{r}
#| label: cpt-cfjeffreyscentposvec
#| echo: true
#| eval: true
set.seed(986)
p <- igccatdist(sample(1:10, size = 5L, replace = TRUE))
q <- igccatdist(sample(1:10, size = 5L, replace = TRUE))
jcent(bind_igc(p,q))
```

Note that the function `lambertW0()` of the package `{lamW}` is used in the backend to compute the Lambert function. Note also that dedicated functions `arithcent()` and `geomcent()` allows for computing arithmetic and geometric centroids of positive vectors.

No closed form expression is known for Jeffreys centroid of probability distributions. Five methods are implemented in `{igcentroids}` to compute approximated values, as made explicit in the documentation of the method `jcent()` for `igcmatcatdistn` objects. In short, the argument `method` of `jcent()` identifies the numerical method to be performed by a character string. 
The approximation returned by  `jcent()` for  `method = "bsa"` relies on the expression of $c_{\mathbb{J}}^{(1)}$ derived by the Lagrangian method in [@nielsen2013]:
$$
c_{\mathbb{J}^{(1)}}(x) = \frac{a(x)}{\mathrm{W}\left( \frac{a(x)}{g(x)} \exp(\lambda +1) \right)}, \quad x \in \mathcal{X},
$$
where $\lambda \leq 0$ is such that $c_{\mathbb{J}}^{(1)} \in \mathcal{P}_{1}(\mathcal{X})$, with no explicit expression for it. The value of $\lambda$ is then approximated by a binary-search algorithm (bsa). 

```{r}
#| label: cpt-bsajeffreyscentpd
r <- igccatdistn(dbinom(0:4, size = 4L, prob = 0.4))
s <- igccatdistn(dbinom(0:4, size = 4L, prob = 0.2))
t <- igccatdistn(dbinom(0:4, size = 4L, prob = 0.1))
mat2 <- bind_igc(r, s, t)
jcent(mat2, method = "bsa",
      tol = 1e-8) # Precision of the bsa is controlled by tol
```
Due to the numerous evaluations of the Lambert function involved in bsa method, this method can be computationnaly expensive, particularly for large state spaces $\mathcal{X}$. An alternative approach consists in iteratively computing arithmetic and geometric means of centroids until convergence. This method, refered to as Gauss-Bregman inductive centering (gbic), has an informational geometric foundation, relying on the dually flat structure of $\mathcal{P}_1(\mathcal{X})$ induced by KL divergence; see @nielsen2024.  Its excellent performances make it the default method used by `jcent()`. Three other methods are also provided, for sake of completeness and comparison purposes. 

```{r}
#| label: cpt-gbicjeffreyscentpd
jcent(mat2, # default corresponds to method = "gbic"
      tol = 1e-8) # tol controls state-by-state approximation error.
```

Package `igcentroids` (version 0.1.0) covers the  computation of Jensen-Shannon centroids only for probability distributions. A numerical approximation of $c_{\mathbb{JS}}^{(1)}$ is obtained by the ConCave-Convexe Procedure (CCCP) introduced by [@yuilleandrangarajan2003], as stated in [@nielsen2020]. See the documentation of the function `jscent()` for details. 

```{r}
#| label: cpt-jscentpd
jscent(mat2)
```


## Clustering categorical distributions {#sec-vig_catdist_clustering}

`{igcentroids}` provides functions for an easy integration of these methods for clustering tasks
using the package `{flexclust}`, as illustrated by the following chunk and @fig-jjsclustering.

```{r}
#| label: fig-jjsclustering
#| echo: true
#| eval: true
#| layout-ncol: 2
#| fig-cap: $k$-medoids clustering performed on a set of 32 randomly generated probaiblity distributions on a three-state space, using Jeffreys and Jensen-Shannon divergences and centroids as measures of dissimarity and centers of classes.
#| fig-subcap:
#|  - Clustering with Jeffreys divergence.
#|  - Clustering with Jensen-Shannon divergence. 
library("flexclust")
# Set jclust family: clustering based on 
# Jeffreys divergence and centroids
# Functions jdivflex(), jcentflex() and undo_igc()
# are included in {igcentroids}
# DO NOT MODIFY the following instruction
jfam <- kccaFamily(name = "jclust",
                   dist = jdivflex,
                   cent = jcentflex,
                   preproc = undo_igc)
# The same for Jensen-Shannon divergence and centroids
jsfam <- kccaFamily(name = "jsclust",
                   dist = jsdivflex,
                   cent = jscentflex,
                   preproc = undo_igc)
# Generate a set of random probability distributions
# Three-state categorical distributions plot
runifsimplex <- function(n = 1L) {
  x <- runif(n)
  y <- runif(n, min = 0, max = 1-x)
  res <- igcmatcatdistn(matrix(c(x,y, 1-x-y), ncol = 3, byrow = FALSE))
  return(res)
}
set.seed(527)
sampsimp <- runifsimplex(n = 32L)
# Operate clustering
res_jeffreys_clust <- kcca(x = sampsimp, 
                           k= 4, # Number of clusters
                           family = jfam)  
# Operate clustering
res_js_clust <- kcca(x = sampsimp, 
                     k= 4, # Number of clusters
                     family = jsfam)  
# Visualize Jeffreys clusters
plot(sampsimp, col = res_jeffreys_clust@cluster+1)
# Add centroids of clusters
points(igcmatcatdistn(res_jeffreys_clust@centers), 
       pch = 4, 
       col = 2:5)
# Visualize Jensen-Shannon clusters
plot(sampsimp, col = res_js_clust@cluster+1)
# Add centroids of clusters
points(igcmatcatdistn(res_js_clust@centers), 
       pch = 4, 
       col = 2:5)


```
We can compute the divergences between the probability distributions and the centroids of the cluster, as illustrated below for the Jeffreys clustering.

```{r}
#| label: cpt-divtocent
cents <- igcmatcatdistn(res_jeffreys_clust@centers) # Centroids
clusters <- split(1:nrow(sampsimp), res_jeffreys_clust@cluster)
jdiv2cents <- list(4)
for (i in 1:4) {
  jdiv2cents[[i]] <- jdiv(p = igcmatcatdistn(sampsimp[clusters[[i]],]), 
                          q = cents)
  colnames(jdiv2cents[[i]]) <- paste0("Centroid_", 1:4)
}
names(jdiv2cents) <- paste0("Cluster_", 1:4)
jdiv2cents

```
